newsitem.title: USA: Republicans push U.S. managed care regulations.
newsitem.headline: Republicans push U.S. managed care regulations.

text.p: Republican lawmakers Wednesday introduced legislation to impose tough new consumer protections on managed care plans, making it more likely Congress may act on the issue during the current session.

The bill sponsored by New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato and Georgia Republican Rep. Charles Norwood would give people the right to choose their own doctors and ensure physicians were not limited in discussing treatment options with patients.

It would also hold plans liable for a patient's wrongful death or personal injuries. That would allow patients in plans covered by the Employee Retirement and Income Security Act of 1974 to sue for malpractice.
Many big company-sponsored health plans are exempt from state insurance laws and regulations under ERISA.

The bill would also require that insurance plans publish and give each patient a list of what they cover, costs and profits and the amount spent on marketing and other non-health costs. Patients would not have to have previous approval to visit hospital emergency rooms.
"The bottom line in medicine must be the health of the patient, not the profits of the company," D'Amato said in a statement.
Roughly 75 percent of insured Americans are now enrolled in managed care plans. As participation has increased, so have complaints about quality of care.
House and Senate Democrats have introduced far more expansive legislation to regulate managed care plans.
President Clinton has also submitted a five-year balanced budget plan to Congress that would cut Medicare pyaments to health maintenance organizations by more than $30 billion over five years.
"In the past we have been very wary of federal mandates having to do with medical issues," said Don White, a spokesman for the American Association of Health Plans, an industry trade organization.
Seeking to head off federal regulations, the Association recently proposed a code of conduct for managed care plans and threatened to sanction those that did not comply.
